name: FloatSong
tagline: A small always-on-top window that shows what is playing and the lyrics that go with it.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: A floating window that reads your current track and scrolls lyrics is not hard logic: it is a frameless always-on-top window, a player API poll, and a lyrics lookup. An agent gets you a working desktop overlay in a sitting. The pain is everything around the edges: each music source needs its own auth or private OS media API, synced lyrics drift without careful offset handling, and a transparent click-through window that behaves across spaces, fullscreen apps and multiple monitors is where most hobby builds quietly fall apart. You will end up supporting exactly one player, probably the one with a public API. That is usually enough for personal use, and clearly less than a shipped app.
coreLoopDIY: Polls your music player for the current track and position, then renders a draggable always-on-top window with time-synced lyrics pulled from a public lyrics API.
requirements: A desktop OS you actually use it on, since this is not a web app
Your own Spotify developer client ID for OAuth, or a local player with a readable media API
whatYouLose: Support for more than one music source without writing each integration yourself
Reliable lyric timing and offset correction, which is fiddlier than it looks
Window behavior that survives fullscreen apps, multiple monitors and OS updates
Visual polish: fonts, fades, blur, the thing that makes an overlay feel native instead of like a browser window on top
Anyone to fix it when a player changes its API
moatNotes: The moat here is taste and platform plumbing, not data. Nothing about it is defensible, it is just annoying to get right.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because overlays live or die on feel. A DIY version will show the right lyrics at roughly the right time in a window that is slightly wrong, and you will notice every day. A paid app is someone else absorbing the OS quirks, the player integrations and the hundred small rendering decisions, usually for less than the cost of a weekend of your own time.
notes: Weekend build, lifetime maintenance, which is the usual trade for desktop utilities.
prompt:
Build a desktop music overlay app in an empty folder.

Stack, no substitutions: Electron with TypeScript, Vite for the renderer, plain CSS. No React, no UI framework, no backend server.

What it does:
1. On launch, open a frameless, transparent, always-on-top window, 420x180, draggable by its background, remembering its last position in a local JSON file.
2. Authenticate to Spotify using OAuth PKCE in the system browser, with a loopback redirect on 127.0.0.1. Read SPOTIFY_CLIENT_ID from .env. Store the refresh token in a local file in the app data directory, never in the repo.
3. Poll the Spotify currently-playing endpoint every 2 seconds. Track title, artist, album art URL, duration and playback position.
4. On track change, fetch synced lyrics from lrclib.net using track, artist and duration. Parse the LRC timestamps. If only plain lyrics exist, show them unsynced. If nothing exists, show the track info alone, not an error dialog.
5. Render the current lyric line large and centered, with the previous and next lines dimmed above and below. Interpolate position between polls using a local timer so scrolling is smooth instead of jumping every 2 seconds.
6. Global hotkeys: Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+L toggles window visibility, Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+K toggles click-through mode so the overlay ignores the mouse.
7. A small settings panel, opened by right-click: font size, opacity, and a manual lyric offset in milliseconds, all persisted locally.

Explicitly out of scope: accounts, cloud sync, telemetry, analytics, auto-update, Apple Music, YouTube Music, mobile, and any lyrics source that needs a paid key.

Ship a README with setup steps, a .env.example containing SPOTIFY_CLIENT_ID, and the exact Spotify app redirect URI to register. Handle token refresh and offline failures by showing the last known state, not by crashing.
